chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Salih ibn al-Sindi from Ja'far ibn Bashir from Khalid ibn 'Umarah from Sadir al-Sayrafi who said:

I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): A hadith reached me from al-Hasan al-Basri; if it is true, then [it is] 'Indeed we belong to Allah and indeed to Him we shall return.' He said: 'And what is it?' I said: It reached me that al-Hasan used to say: 'If the heat of the sun boiled his brain, he would not seek shade behind the wall of a money-changer; and if his liver cracked from thirst, he would not ask for water from the house of a money-changer, while it is my work and my trade, and in it my flesh and blood grew, and from it my Hajj and 'Umrah.' Then he sat and said: 'Al-Hasan lied. Take evenly and give evenly. When the prayer time arrives, leave what is in your hand and rise for the prayer. Do you not know that the Companions of the Cave were money-changers?'

key_terms.خُذْ سَوَاءً وَأَعْ سَوَاءً: Take evenly and give evenly (principle of fair exchange)

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Baqir say about the piety and trade practices of money-changers (sayyarifa)?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) refutes the exaggerated piety of al-Hasan al-Basri regarding money-changers, who claimed their trade did not distract them from spiritual needs. The Imam corrects this by emphasizing practical justice in commerce ('take evenly, give evenly') and prioritizing the immediacy of prayer over transactional completion. He notably cites the Companions of the Cave (Ahl al-Kahf) as money-changers, linking their worldly profession to their eventual spiritual retreat, thereby validating trade as a legitimate sphere for believers.
